The Release to Rescue initiative aims to cut ambulance handover times at hospitals

A two-hour ambulance handover limit at emergency departments is going to be "very challenging" to achieve this winter, according to a senior doctor.

The Release to Rescue initiative was introduced this year to ensure a maximum two-hour wait for patients and to free up crews to respond to calls more quickly.

But more than 2,000 ambulance handovers breached the two-hour wait time between May and August, the first four full months of the scheme.

The Department of Health said the scheme had delivered "improvements", with more than 6,000 waits of two hours or more in the same period last year.

William Murphy, 85, waited over 12 hours for an ambulance after falling ill at his home in County Down in September.

His son Ronnie said they were told over the phone that the ambulance service was "under pressure" and that a crew would come as soon as possible.

"Dad was deteriorating still at that stage. He was completely off his feet, he couldn't walk," said Ronnie.

"I was concerned - the length of time it was taking and Mum was ringing but they were just saying still the same message.

William Murphy had to wait 12 hours before an ambulance arrived at his home

"Whenever he got into hospital he had to go onto oxygen and his oxygen levels were severely low.

"Had there been another emergency, had my dad took more seriously ill, where would we have been?"

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) has apologised to William for the "delay experienced following his 999 call".

"The demand for our services exceeds our capacity to respond in as timely a manner as we would like," it said.

The Release to Rescue protocol had "delivered some benefits", it said - but it accepted that "more focus is required to reduce the turnaround times even further".

Ronnie was unhappy that his father spent almost two days in the Ulster Hospital's emergency department before he was admitted to a ward - but added that he had no complaints about the care he received.

"The floor, the waiting area in the new A&E - every seat was filled," he said.

"There was people sitting on the floors; there was people all sitting everywhere; there was people lying on the floors; there was people crying, families in distress".

Ronnie Murphy said his father's health deteriorated while they waited for an ambulance

The South Eastern Health Trust said it was "sorry to hear of the experience" Ronnie and his family described.

Dr Michael Perry from the Royal College of Emergency Medicine said a protocol limiting ambulance handovers to two hours should not be required.

"If we had a flowing system where patients moved in a timely fashion [through the hospital system], where there was space in emergency departments, ambulances would offload as soon as they arrive," said Perry.

"We're now coming into the colder winter months, where we do get increased demand on our emergency departments because of normal seasonal winter illnesses.

Dr Michael Perry said hospitals should have a "flowing system" for patients

"And we're expecting that pressure to get even higher again on us.

"To meet the requirement to offload ambulances in that timely fashion, it's going to be very challenging for us."

Norman Cunningham, a Unite union representative for the NIAS, said resolving patient flow problems in hospitals would be difficult.

"There will never be a quick fix with health because demand, particularly for the ambulance service, goes up 3% to 5% a year," said Cunningham.

"The problem for us is not so much the waiting outside hospital, which is disastrous for an ambulance service, but it's the people waiting at home who are seriously ill, who are relying on an ambulance getting to them, but it can't get to them."

The Department of Health has asked all six health trusts, including the ambulance service, to make savings of up to 12% over three years .

According to a NIAS savings plan published in August, £5.2m of cuts to its 2026-27 budget are "dependent on the successful continuation" of Release to Rescue.

The document warns that if other trusts "withdraw or reduce the operational measures supporting Release to Rescue" as part of their own savings plans, "there will be a direct impact on NIAS capacity, response performance and expenditure".

The Department of Health said that "severe pressures" on emergency departments created "additional challenges to implement the Release to Rescue protocol".

But it said that the protocol had "shown significant success so far", with a reduction in ambulance response and handover times across the health service.

Norman Cunningham said demand for ambulances increases every year

The South Eastern Health Trust said it "intermittently paused" the protocol at the Ulster Hospital on 1 September after an "exceptionally busy" bank holiday Monday, with 23 ambulances breaching the two-hour limit.

That was the only time so far that a health trust has paused the policy.

The trust said it had made "significant progress" in improving ambulance handover times, with 90% "turned around in under two hours" in August.

The Southern Health Trust said there had been no decision to pause the protocol at its emergency departments - but it "may on occasion be breached due to day-to-day service pressures."

The Northern Health Trust said it had "never stepped down the protocol", while the Western Health Trust and the Belfast Health Trust both said they had not paused it since its introduction.

A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

McDonald's workers speak out over sexual abuse claims

McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'

Every McDonald's warned over staff sexual abuse

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Ex-McDonald's worker: "You need to fix it so it doesn't happen again"

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.

The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.

Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.

Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''

She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.

"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"

The claims were presented by law firm Leigh Day, which is acting for the current and former employees.

The claims focus on the vulnerability of young or female workers in the workplace and follow allegations of widespread harassment and discrimination across McDonald's restaurants in the UK.

Leigh Day partner Kiran Daurka told the BBC: "We're really delighted that the judge has found that these claims can go forward to a full hearing. It's really important for access to justice that these cases are heard."

A McDonald's spokesperson said they could not comment on the specifics of ongoing legal proceedings.

In a statement, they said the company had "embedded an extensive set of robust and far-reaching initiatives" as part of its "steadfast commitment" to its staff, adding that this work continues.

"Any form of harassment, discrimination or inappropriate behaviour is unacceptable and has no place in our restaurants or offices. We are confident that with the guidance and partnership of external experts, we and our franchisees have industry leading safeguarding measures in place," the spokesperson added.

Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack

The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.

The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.

The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November

It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China .

Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.

At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".

President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine

Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.

That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.

Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.

Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

Sotheby's staff handle the "Châtaigniers en fleurs" painting by Vincent van Gogh at an auction preview in Hong Kong last month

Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).

The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.

The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.

Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'

It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.

The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.

Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.

Four other owners then had the painting.

The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

Rwanda’s Minister of Defence, Juvenal Marizamunda, held discussions with government officials and representatives of international organisations attending the 2026 Schuman Security and Defence Forum in Brussels, Belgium.

The third edition of the forum took place on November 17 and 18, bringing together senior decision-makers from more than 80 partner countries, EU member states, international and regional organisations, think tanks and academic institutions.

Organised by the European Union, the forum provided a platform for exchanging views on shared security challenges and possible responses.

This year’s theme focused on “reliable security and defence partnerships in times of growing threats and uncertainty.” The programme included a ministerial dinner, keynote speeches and sessions examining how existing and future partnerships could respond to current and emerging security threats.

Marizamunda’s meetings with fellow delegates took place alongside discussions on international security and defence cooperation. Details of the specific issues raised in his talks were not disclosed.

Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the campaign's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.

Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.

Democrats won control of the Senate and House, while Texas, Ohio and other states swung away from Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living.

Musk was speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.

"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.

He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.

One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.

According to BBC analysis , Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.

Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.

Democrats have vowed greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the roll out of controversial data centres.

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit

Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.

Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.

And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.

Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.

His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.

But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines

First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fourth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.

However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.

Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fourth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives

The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.

Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.

Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.

The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.

Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025

This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.

Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.

Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.

But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.

Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.

There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.

Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.

The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.

So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.

For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.

But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.

A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy

He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

Councillors Ian Middleton and Fiona Mawson are concerned about the loss of hedgerows and trees

Work to gain access to land for a housing development and a new "super cycleway" has resulted in "environmental vandalism", councillors have said.

Kidlington Green councillors Ian Middleton and Fiona Mawson said residents were concerned by the number of hedgerows and trees recently cut down on Oxford Road.

Adjacent fields have planning permission for 800 homes as part of wider plans for more than 4,400 to be built in the area.

A spokesperson for developer Bellway said all the work had been done with an ecologist on site and complied with outline planning consent.

The trees and hedgerows were cut back on land next to the Oxford Road

The cycleway would help connecting Kidlington to Oxford, running alongside the A4165, Oxford Road.

The route is expected to get busier with significant growth planned for north Oxford, including a potential new stadium for Oxford United.

According to Bellway, the trees and hedges were cut down between 26 October and 6 November to "create access" to the site planned for housing, as well as to "facilitate" the work for the cycleway.

The proposals include "significant landscaping and ecological enhancements" as well as 50% affordable housing and "other infrastructure", it said.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

Middleton, the lead member for housing and greener communities at Cherwell District Council, said outline planning permission did not give the developer "unrestricted permission to carry out works".

He also said its actions were "nonsensical" and premature, given the cycle path was not "imminent".

"If all they needed was access, why have they ripped out an entire hedgerow?" he said.

"We knew some of this was going to be taken out, but it's the scale of it that's really impacted people and sent shock waves across the local community."

A spokesperson for Bellway said hit had been working with Cherwell District Council "to agree details of a replacement wildlife corridor," including planting 150 new trees.

Yabaye icyamamare aho atuye kubera umukino w'igisoro.

Rosalia Mukandekezi utuye mu karere ka Kamonyi mu ntara y'amajyepfo ni umwe mu bagore mbarwa bakina umukino w'igisoro (cyangwa urubugu mu Kirundi).

Uyu mukecuru avuga ko amaze imyaka isaga 50 akina uyu mukino, avuga ko usa n'aho ari karande mu muryango we.

Uretse gukina byo kwishimisha no gusabana n'abandi, Mukandekezi, w'imyaka 65, anitabira amarushanwa y'uyu mukino ndetse amaze no kwegukana imidari ku rwego rw'igihugu.

Mu gace k'icyaro ka Karama, mu karere ka Kamonyi, ni ho Mukandekezi atuye.

Iwe uhasanga urujya n'uruza rw'abantu, cyane cyane abakuze, bagenzwa no gukina na we igisoro.

Igisoro ni umukino gakondo ubu usa n'ugenda ucika dore ko benshi mu bato nta bumenyi na busa bawufiteho, mu bihe byo hambere wasaga n'umwihariko w'abagabo.

Yagize ati: "Natangiye kuwukina nkiri akana gato k'imyaka nka 10. Data na we navutse awukina. Yatubwiraga ko bajyaga kuwukina ibwami ndetse ko hari n'abagore bacye bawukinaga ariko bo bakajya mu gikari. Ni we watumye unshishikaza."

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Mukandekezi avuga ko yavukiye i Nyanza ku gicumbi cy'umuco – hahoze ari ibwami – ariko ubu atuye mu karere ka Kamonyi.

Ubuhanga bwa Mukandekezi muri uyu mukino bwatumye agira igitinyiro ndetse agera n'aho ahagararira akarere n'intara muri uyu mukino ku rwego rw'igihugu.

Agira ati: "Ku karere batangiye amarushanwa y'Umurenge Kagame Cup baravuga ngo niba hari n'umugore uhari ntasigare. Ngiye ndatsinda mu rwego rw'intara."

Yerekana umudari w'umuringa (bronze) avuga ko yatsindiye mu mwaka wa 2023 mu marushanwa yari yabereye i Huye, na ho ho muri iyo ntara y'amajyepfo, ndetse n'undi mudari yatsindiye mu 2024 mu marushanwa yabereye i Rubavu, mu burengerazuba bw'igihugu.

Ubwo namusuraga aho atuye mu gace k'icyaro k'umurenge wa Karama, nasanze Mukandekezi arimo kubuguza na Elias Usabuwera waba nk'umuhungu we. Namubajije uko uyu mukecuru abonwa muri aka gace.

Ati: "Kubera mukecuru asa n'aho ari we ucyizi [igisoro] wenyine, ubona bisa n'ibidasanzwe. Baba bavuga bati 'uyu muntu uzi igisoro ari umubyeyi...'"

Urugo rwa Mukandekezi, ruri hafi y'umuhanda, rwabaye nk'ihuriro ry'ibyiciro byose, cyane cyane mu masaha y'umugoroba ubwo abantu baba bakitse imirimo.

Umusaza Valens Hategekimana ni umwe mu bahansanze aje gukina. Na we avuga ko afitiye icyubahiro uyu mukecuru ubona bari mu kigero kimwe cy'imyaka.

Yagize ati: "Iyo yaduserukiye tuba dufite igishyika cyinshi, tubaza amakuru buri kanya. Yatsinda tugakomera amashyi rimwe. Nkanjye iyo antsinze numva akantu k'ipfunwe gato ariko umuvuno namuhaye ugatuma atsinda sinongera kuwumuha. Nanjye nkamugaragura!"

Ku batazi iby'uyu mukino bashobora kuwufata nk'uwo gutakaza igihe gusa ariko Mukandekezi avuga ko umufatiye runini no ku buzima bwe.

"Uyu mukino utuma nduhuka mu mutwe. Nka twe bakuru hari igihe uba utekereza byinshi ariko iyo uri gukina urabyibagirwa.

"Ikindi uyu mukino utuma dusabana. Nk'ubu mba mpamagara nk'abantu b'i Rusizi twahujwe n'igisoro... Igihe cyose nzaba ngihumeka nzakomeza kuwukina."

Igisoro ni umukino benshi mu bato batazi ndetse utanagaragara ku rutonde rw'iyo leta y'u Rwanda ishyiramo imbaraga.

Gusa abatsimbaraye ku muco bo bashobora kuba batakwifuza ko wazima. Mukandekezi avuga ko harimo gutegurwa uburyo yakwifatanya n'abandi mu kwigisha uyu mukino kugira ngo utazacika burundu.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Meet the SPOTY Men's Footballer of the Year contenders

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024

The Games Rating Authority, based in Stevenage, gets to play the games long before release

The latest Grand Theft Auto game brings the franchise's trademark violence and adult storytelling to the latest generation of gaming hardware.

But long before its release, examiners at the Games Rating Authority , external (GRA), based in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, got to play the game to decide its appropriate age rating.

They analysed its content before assigning a PEGI age rating , external of 18, which covers 38 European territories.

But who decides a game is for adults only, and how do they make that decision?

The Games Rating Authority administers PEGI age ratings on physical games in Europe

Video games experience a similar process to films shown in UK cinemas, where examiners from the British Board of Film Classification watch each film before deciding its rating.

But rating games presents a unique challenge.

Modern games can contain huge worlds that take months to explore. Some allow players to make their own choices, meaning two people can have vastly different experiences.

Developers first complete a GRA questionnaire disclosing any contentious content and provide at least two hours of footage, along with transcripts of the game's dialogue.

Examiners study this material, logging timestamps for instances of blood, gore, horror, drug use or bad language.

Examiner Sadie West is a fan of role-playing video games

Lifelong gamer Sadie West joined the GRA believing it would be the dream job: being paid to play games.

She says: "I definitely look at it more analytically when I'm playing here.

"Since I've started here, I play games a lot less at home, but because I play in such a different way at work to what I'm playing at home, I can still enjoy it."

West uses her skills with a controller to explore choices and scenarios that developers may not have captured on video.

She says: "Things like, is there an NPC (non-playable character) that I can go up to, and can I attack them? Can I hurt this person? Or what happens if my character jumps off a bridge?

"Sometimes I die on purpose to see what a character death would look like."

Many games, like Grand Theft Auto VI, feature large sprawling worlds for players to explore

When playing games in her own time West hates hurting NPCs, but admits at work: "Unfortunately I have to be a bit evil sometimes".

She will typically play a game for several days, checking for blood, suggestive costumes and potentially exploitative in-game purchases.

She says: "Once I'm happy that I've seen everything that would impact the rating, I then go through and I write up a report."

That report is kept on record, while a version without plot spoilers is shared online for parents and players to read.

Examiners follow strict classification criteria overseen by a panel that includes child welfare experts and psychologists.

Ian Rice, director general of the GRA, says the criteria ensure ratings are applied "consistently and fairly".

Violence is only one element that is analysed, but shows how context can affect the classification:

PEGI 3 & 7: Child-friendly, cartoon-like violence, such as in Minecraft, Rocket League, Roblox or Mario.

PEGI 12: Unrealistic violence between humans, this could be games like Fortnite which have no blood or injury detail.

PEGI 16: Realistic violence between humans, can include visible blood and pain reactions.

PEGI 18: These games include what is classified as "gross violence", with high levels of blood and gore, or violence directed at innocent civilians.

Sexually graphic content and the glamorisation of illegal drug use also trigger an automatic 18 rating.

Some might wonder why games need adult content at all. Rice points out games can cover mature themes just like other forms of storytelling.

He says: "Just because it's in a game doesn't mean somebody's making light of it.

"They can cover serious issues, just like Netflix shows or any other kind of media."

Games Rating Authority director general Ian Rice says his children have "stolen" his consoles but he gets to "pull rank" to play some games in the office

Since the GRA began administering PEGI ratings in 2012, it has only refused to classify one title , making it illegal to sell it in the UK.

Rice says the authority maintains a dialogue with developers and offers advice throughout the development process.

He says: "That back and forth is really important because they have the opportunity during the development process to change things like the virtual camera angles that particular scenes are shown at, they can cut out words, they can cut out scenes."

Rice himself is a keen gamer, but as a parent he is keen to stress the importance of the age rating system.

Rice adds: "Every child is different, and parents know their children best.

"Our ask is to use the PEGI ratings, the information, and the descriptors to make an informed decision... but if we're rating a game as an 18, we really feel it is only acceptable for adults only."

Ten games into the Premier League season, the top five places are dominated by big six clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton , a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United , Liverpool , Manchester City , Arsenal , Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool , Arsenal and United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea , Manchester City and Tottenham .

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.

We will use Everton , the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.

So what has driven this huge escalation?

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool , told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."

Only 10% of Everton 's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

It means Everton , and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham , and £200m below Liverpool and City.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal .

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea 's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea , rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs , thanks to their new ground, by £85m.

" Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

" Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."

Chelsea 's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.

"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."

The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton , Brentford , Bournemouth , Crystal Palace , Fulham and Leeds ," Maguire said.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent £3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the £3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under £100m."

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford , Brighton , Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than £40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle , the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are £60m and £70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.

The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending £945m on players in the past five years.

The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

The damaged boat washed ashore on Senegal's coast

Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.

Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the town of Yenne. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.

The incident comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.

Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).

"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.

A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five people, the AFP reported.

Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school item believed to be associated with a high school student.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.

He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.

Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.

Thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty.

The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances this year along the Atlantic route off Western African coast this year alone.

It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.

James McAtee made six appearances for Manchester City after coming through the academy

"James McAtee is probably one of the winners of this pre-season."

Oliver Glasner's immediate impression of his Nottingham Forest midfielder foretold the faith the head coach has shown in him.

Forest appear to have found their Elliot Anderson replacement from within as McAtee has become a key man for the Austrian.

After his £30m move from Manchester City in 2025, McAtee endured a difficult start to life at the City Ground.

Yet he played a key role as Forest toppled City and the returning Anderson before the international break for their first home win of the season.

There has been no clamour for an England call, but has Thomas Tuchel unfairly overlooked McAtee - and how has he gone from the Forest bench to indispensable?

The City academy graduate made only two Premier League starts last season, one of the bigger victims of Forest's revolving door as the club went through four managers.

Nine starts in Forest's run to the Europa League semi-finals could not hide a campaign of frustration.

It was supposed to be a platform after captaining England Under-21s to Euro 2025 victory, but he played only 289 minutes in the league.

The 24-year-old has already tripled those minutes this season after becoming a key player for Glasner, starting every top-flight game.

It followed the manager suggesting in the summer that McAtee could replace Anderson following his £116m move to City - something which left McAtee unsure.

"When I first came in and [Glasner] put me in the [number] six [role] on the second day in my head I was like: 'oh, he's not seeing me in his plans, I'm playing deeper'," he said at Forest's training ground.

"My confidence is growing, but not fully there yet, but I think we're on our way.

"I thought I had it in my locker, but I never thought he would actually try it out with me in pre-season.

"I think Ibra [Sangare] was injured at the time so I was thinking, I'm just going in for Ibra. But then as pre-season got on and I was playing there I felt more comfortable."

Forest fan impressed by 'surprise' player who stepped into Elliot Anderson's shoes

It was evidence of McAtee's work after he worked throughout the summer to return for pre-season.

He trained with former Plymouth, Leeds and Ipswich midfielder David Norris, now a personal trainer, and put on 2.5kg of muscle while losing 1kg of fat.

Weight sessions followed fitness work in the morning, which is what prompted Glasner to credit his summer of work.

The relationship with Glasner has been crucial. The Forest boss has offered clarity and calmness to a squad which endured the chaos last season.

A post-match inquest following the 2-0 defeat by Brentford sparked the right response from the squad, after a start which has left them 16th in the league.

After McAtee failed to find consistency and rhythm last season, Glasner promised him he would be afforded time and the benefit of the doubt if he had a poor game.

"I think [last season] was a me problem. I was struggling to get my chance," he said, having used a psychologist before the start of pre-season.

"I've never really had a season like that, I was always in and out. It was frustrating, but as frustrating as it was, it was a good lesson.

"As I saw my confidence kept going worse and worse and worse. As I've watched clips of me, I can tell when I was going a little bit under.

"This year, if I make a pass and I lose it, it won't bother me as much because I've been through that."

McAtee has always had supporters at the City Ground. All four managers were impressed by his training levels last season, but he was always under pressure to deliver when given a brief chance.

Forest technical director George Syrianos has also championed the calls internally for McAtee.

It has allowed McAtee - whose brother John plays for Bolton - to feel the faith, having learned from previous difficulties, with England on his mind.

He is eager to make the step up to Tuchel's senior side, and has supporters at the Football Association.

He prioritised playing for the U21s at Euro 2025 - captaining them to victory - over going to the Club World Cup with City, and underlined his determination to represent his country to manager Pep Guardiola and director of football Txiki Begiristain at the time.

Now, under Glasner, after a difficult first season, McAtee has that platform with Euro 2028 a realistic target.

"At this moment I need to have a good year for me to maybe be in with the chance of getting picked, but the competition in the position I'm playing is so high," he said.

"If I could add some goals, some stats, it could put me within a chance to be around that circle. The competition is very elite at the moment, but that's the aim, that's the goal."

James McAtee had two previous spells on loan at Sheffield United

Against City, he was moved further forward, with Ryan Yates coming in to add more bodies in midfield.

But the stats back up McAtee's improvement and he compares favourably to others.

He has made the most final-third passes for Forest (151) and has played the joint-most through balls with Morgan Gibbs-White (five). His 426 passes are behind only Murillo's 501, and he has created 18 chances - six short of Gibbs-White.

McAtee is only 29m behind Gibbs-White, having carried the ball 1,180m this season, but has made the most carries with 109 and has won possession back 63 times - winning 53% of his ground duels, indicating he has developed more of a mean streak in his game.

He has comfortably outperformed Everton 's James Garner - one of his rivals for a place in the England squad - creating more chances, making more forward passes, winning more defensive duels and making more successful tackles.

McAtee has also made more recoveries, successful tackles, passes and clearances than Crystal Palace 's Adam Wharton.

Now, having gone under the radar this season, come the next international break in March, Tuchel may not be able to ignore him.

"I'm seeing this as a different side of myself, I'm so much more confident on the pitch, I'm so much more comfortable," adds McAtee. "It's like two different players."

There were 22 people on board the Bayesian at the time of the incident

The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about a critical safety risk that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas , 59.

Mike Lynch and his daughter Hannah both died when the Bayesian sank

Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."

Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.

The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".

In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.

In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.

With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).

The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

A study commissioned by the MAIB indicated that, in the conditions assessed, Bayesian was vulnerable to extreme winds at the vessel's widest point, known as the beam.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.

The wreackage of the Bayesian off the coast of Porticello, Sicily

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.

Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.

They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.

The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.

Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.

The MAIB's final report into the sinking, published on Thursday, appeared to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecution experts have reportedly blamed errors by the crew rather than problems with the yacht.

The investigation was carried out alongside a criminal probe in Italy , where captain James Cutfield, chief engineer Tim Parker Eaton and deckhand Matthew Griffith are under investigation over potential charges of multiple manslaughter and culpable shipwreck.

British investigators said that Italian prosecutors had restricted access to some witnesses and evidence.

"It is possible that the circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence withheld by the Italian authorities," the report says.

However, the MAIB's Graves said he was satisfied with the British investigation.

"We are content with our investigation, the investigation that we've undertaken, and the information we've used to feed into it."

The report also found that alcohol consumption had not contributed to the sinking.

MAIB investigator Simon Graves: "This was an accident and there were a number of contributory factors"

The MAIB report makes seven recommendations to four agencies. It calls for new regulations to be set for single-hulled sailing vessels, and new rules around life rafts.

It also urges collaboration between the Met Office and its global counterpart to improve information-sharing of severe weather forecasts with mariners.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

Bududa, eastern Uganda, has suffered repeated deadly landslides, including disasters in 2010 and 2018 that killed more than 142 people.

Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.

The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.

Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.

The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.

The landslide struck Bududa in 2019, killing more than 53 people, including 33 children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.

William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family members.

"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."

The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.

"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.

The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.

They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.

Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.

"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.

The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.

In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.

The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.

"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.

She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.

"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.

Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.

Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18 million Ugandan shillings ($4,300) to help them move to safer areas.

But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.

Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8 million shillings ($1,900), plus 10 million shillings (about $2,400) towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.

The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.

The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.

But the complainants say relocation must involve more than move people out of danger.

They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.

The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

The top 10 European strikers of the 21st century

Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.

There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.

This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.

Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.

We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.

So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.

Top 10 European Strikers of the Century - Part One

Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.

Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'."

Honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player."

Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.

The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.

Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher."

Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries."

Zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.

Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think."

Laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible."

Honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that."

The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.

Honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi."

Balague: "What could have been, yes. He was the national team's record scorer too before Harry Kane took it. I find him to deserve this place as he had to adapt to a lot of strikers and he did it well. He had the ability to link up and score. He was very intelligent."

Laurens: "He is the most street footballer England has ever seen. There's no rules, that kind of anger you saw on the pitch. I don't think people in England realise how good he was."

What does becoming the all-time World Cup top goalscorer get you? Sixth place on the best European strikers this century list. The Real Madrid forward, 27, just misses out on the top five.

Laurens: "Maybe if we do this ranking again in a few years he will be higher. I would have had him top five, for sure. He has scored more than 400 goals. I don't think Messi and Ronaldo had scored that many at that age, so he's ahead. I don't know if he will play for as long as them but he hasn't done much wrong in his career."

Balague: "This list has to do what you feel about the player, not science - 22 goals in 22 appearances in World Cups and [Euro] Championships. He should be at least top three because of that. Great stats, but we're not in love with him."

Honigstein: " I don't think there is a forward that is as good as footballer as him in 2026. On that basis alone he should be higher, but people when they vote have other things in their head. The only way to win everyone over is to score more goals and win more World Cups for France, which I think is possible."

There was little between Mbappe and Erling Haaland, but it is Manchester City's prolific Norwegian who slips in at fifth. The 26-year-old has already scored more than 300 club goals and has a staggering 68 in 61 games for his country.

Balague: "Mbappe should be higher than him. Haaland scored 52 goals in 53 games [in 2022-23], that is astonishing, but he's gone 11 finals without scoring. We're talking about the best. We're talking about what we see at the moment and what we see is someone who is calculated but in a more charming way. An ability to score we haven't seen in a while; power, ability to finish. He is not world class to the level of others."

Honigstein: "I don't think it's fair to judge him on just that. They [Manchester City] won the Champions League when he was there. When Haaland arrived with Pep Guardiola, they found a way to do it. What makes him unique is the physical attributes and the pace. To have both is unique. He can sprint like a 100m sprinter. Is he the fifth best striker of the 21st Century? I don't think he's that far behind."

Interesting, this, because Robert Lewandowski is well clear of Haaland in fourth, but the leap from the Polish forward to the top three is massive - more than 10,000 votes.

The 38-year-old is still chipping away for Chicago Fire in Major League Soccer, having been a reliably ruthless assassin for Barcelona, Bayern and Dortmund.

Honigstein: "He used to play basketball, judo, handball - his father wanted him to have a wholesome education. You could see his completeness that he had as a centre-forward. Nothing in his game was extraordinary but in terms of ticking all the boxes, none come close to him."

Balague: "He said he learned to be an elite striker when he forgot what he had just done, like a fish. Mistakes he had in his head affected his performance. One day he just continued like it didn't matter."

Laurens: "He won the Ballon d'Or in Covid, it won't be on his mantlepiece but we all know it was his."

Fresh from his Ballon d'Or triumph, England's record goalscorer and appearance maker rides into the top three on the back of 61 goals in 51 outings for Bayern Munich last season.

Kane left the Premier League three years ago with the second-most goals ever in the competition, and is also Tottenham's all-time record scorer.

Honigstein: "Third place, at least. He is doing incredible things. At 33, still not quite at his peak. I don't think he relies on his pace, physicality, it's all about intelligence, technique. I don't think there's anyone in the game that strikes a ball as well as him right now. I don't think any player comes close that we've talked about so far in overall work-rate, defending, helping the team, making tackles in your box in the 90th minute when you're 3-0 up because he's that kind of guy. He is humble and a superb human being."

Laurens: "What I love about Kane, from a young age, a lot of this list you just knew the trajectory would be all the way to the top. Kane was not like that. It could have been very different for him. Nobody at 17 would've said he was going to win the Ballon d'Or. Nobody believed in him like the others. Kane had a very different journey."

Runner-up Thierry Henry is the only striker in the top six who is retired. A World Cup and Euros winner with France, Henry won titles with Arsenal - where he scored 228 goals - and a Champions League with Barcelona.

Honigstein: "During his time, I don't think there was a player like him in the Premier League. The way he played football was stylish, elegant, but there was almost a kind of a romantic connection between him and the ball. I don't think there was anyone near that kind of level of technique and, for want of a better word, va-va-voom he exuded. That just made for amazing viewing."

Laurens: "For me as a fellow Parisien, he's a very special player, a very special man. A career that has been incredible from a young age. It's that season in the Premier League - 24 goals, 20 assists in 38 games - not even Kane or Benzema or Cristiano, OK, Messi is different, but they haven't done that and yet he did it.

"There are still some people who undervalue him and underappreciate him and the monster that he was on the football pitch. He had it all. The pace, the style, the elegance, the technique, the mentality, the goals, the aura, the charisma. Just everything you wanted if you were to build a striker. One of the greatest football brains ever."

Of course, at number one, it's the man chasing the 1,000-goal dream. Cristiano Ronaldo may have retired from Portugal duty with 146 notches on his strike chart but the quest goes on at Al-Nassr.

The 41-year-old's evolution from tricky winger to prolific frontman has taken him from Sporting to Manchester United, twice, Real Madrid, Juventus and now Saudi Arabia.

Balague: "He's the best striker in history. His numbers are incredible. He won't stop until he gets to 1,000. He is somebody who is special. We know his background, how he wanted to be Ballon d'Or winner at 12 and didn't stop until he got there. He ran up the mountains of Funchal with weights in his ankles and snuck into the gym when it was closed to get the physique he wanted."

Laurens: "Always in the right place at the right time. The instinct. He was born with a gift, like all in this list. But you still have to work hard. Nobody will ever reach those levels again. 1,000 goals for club and country will never be done again, I think."

Honigstein: "Peak Ronaldo for me was Gareth Bale scoring and him looking very unhappy. I don't think there will be any dispute about him being the greatest. Somebody who has done it all, won it all, and he's still going for the love of it."
